claim: Normal pancreatic islets contain a subset of proinsulin molecules bearing at least one free cysteine thiol.
source: Remarkably, normal pancreatic islets contain a subset of proinsulin molecules bearing at least one free cysteine thiol.
evidence: Demonstrated by AMS alkylation experiments showing band shifts in human and rodent islets (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)

claim: In human or rodent islets with a perturbed ER folding environment, non-native proinsulin enters intermolecular disulfide-linked complexes.
source: In human (or rodent) islets with a perturbed endoplasmic reticulum folding environment, non-native proinsulin enters intermolecular disulfide-linked complexes.
evidence: Shown by nonreducing SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting after PERK inhibitor treatment or BiP depletion (Figures 1B, 3A, 3C, 3D)

claim: In genetically obese mice with otherwise wild-type islets, disulfide-linked complexes of proinsulin are more abundant.
source: In genetically obese mice with otherwise wild-type islets, disulfide-linked complexes of proinsulin are more abundant, and leptin receptor-deficient mice, the further increase of such complexes tracks with the onset of islet insulin deficiency and diabetes.
evidence: Demonstrated in LepRdb/db mice and LepR-Nkx2.1 KO mice by nonreducing SDS-PAGE showing >90% of proinsulin in disulfide-linked complexes (Figures 4D, 4E, 5C)

claim: Proinsulin-Cys(B19) and Cys(A20) are necessary and sufficient for the formation of proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes.
source: Proinsulin-Cys(B19) and Cys(A20) are necessary and sufficient for the formation of proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes
evidence: Demonstrated by expressing mutant proinsulins retaining only specific cysteine pairs; only keep-B19/A20 efficiently recreated the full ladder of disulfide-linked complexes (Figure 6C)

claim: Proinsulin Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) covalent homodimers resist reductive dissociation.
source: indeed, proinsulin Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) covalent homodimers resist reductive dissociation, highlighting a structural basis for aberrant proinsulin complex formation.
evidence: Shown by expressing single-cysteine proinsulin mutants; keep-B19 formed dimers that could not be broken at room temperature in SDS-gel sample buffer even with 200 mM DTT (Figure 7A)

claim: Increased proinsulin misfolding via disulfide-linked complexes is an early event associated with prediabetes that worsens with β-cell dysfunction in type two diabetes.
source: We conclude that increased proinsulin misfolding via disulfide-linked complexes is an early event associated with prediabetes that worsens with ß-cell dysfunction in type two diabetes.
evidence: Demonstrated in LepRdb/db mice where disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes were increased before onset of diabetes (blood glucose 101-118 mg/dL) and persisted through disease progression (Figures 4D, 5C)

claim: Native proinsulin folding requires formation of Cys(B7)-Cys(A7), Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) and Cys(A6)-Cys(A11) disulfide pairs.
source: Native proinsulin folding requires formation of Cys(B7)-Cys(A7), Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) and Cys(A6)-Cys(A11) disulfide pairs (Haataja et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: No modification by AMS could be detected in secreted recombinant human proinsulin or proinsulin from rodent islets or INS cells.
source: As examined by immunoblotting with anti-proinsulin antibody, no modification by AMS could be detected in secreted recombinant human proinsulin or proinsulin from rodent islets, or INS cells (e.g., Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by AMS alkylation experiments on secreted proinsulin showing no band shift

claim: Alkylation of intracellular proinsulin with AMS in human islets caused a decrease in unmodified proinsulin accompanied by the appearance of proinsulin alkylated on at least one cysteine thiol.
source: Remarkably, however, alkylation of intracellular proinsulin with AMS in human islets caused a decrease in unmodified proinsulin accompanied by the appearance of proinsulin alkylated on at least one cysteine thiol (Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown by AMS alkylation experiments with band shifts detected by immunoblotting

claim: The presence of a free thiol in a significant subpopulation of proinsulin molecules can lead to inappropriate intermolecular disulfide attack on neighboring proinsulin molecules.
source: The presence of a free thiol in a significant subpopulation of proinsulin molecules can lead to inappropriate intermolecular disulfide attack on neighboring proinsulin molecules (Cunningham et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2010a; Liu et al., 2007; Wang et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: Inhibition of PERK dramatically increased the intracellular accumulation of proinsulin and shifted its distribution to the classic impacted-ER phenotype.
source: Moreover, whereas inhibition of PERK dramatically increased the intracellular accumulation of proinsulin and shifted its distribution to the classic impacted-ER phenotype (Figure 1C) (Gupta et al., 2010), a remarkable ladder of higher molecular mass bands appeared upon Western blotting with mAb anti-proinsulin after nonreducing SDS-PAGE (Figure 1B left).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy and Western blotting after PERK inhibitor treatment

claim: Despite increased intracellular proinsulin after PERK inhibition, secretion of proinsulin to the medium was not increased.
source: Despite this increase of intracellular proinsulin, secretion of proinsulin to the medium was not increased
evidence: Shown by comparing cell lysate and media samples after PERK inhibitor treatment (Figure 1B)

claim: Secreted proinsulin was recovered exclusively as the monomeric form by nonreducing SDS-PAGE, demonstrating efficient quality control in the secretory pathway.
source: furthermore, by nonreducing SDS-PAGE, secreted proinsulin was recovered exclusively as the monomeric form (Figure 1B right), demonstrating efficient quality control in the secretory pathway.
evidence: Shown by nonreducing SDS-PAGE of secreted proinsulin showing only monomeric form

claim: The intracellular accumulation of a ladder of proinsulin immunoreactive species upon nonreducing SDS-PAGE was not detected by conventional Western blotting with polyclonal anti-insulin.
source: The intracellular accumulation of a ladder of proinsulin immunoreactive species upon nonreducing SDS-PAGE was not detected by conventional Western blotting with polyclonal anti-insulin, despite that this antibody identifies both proinsulin and proinsulin conversion intermediates (Figure 1D left).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing Western blots with anti-insulin versus anti-proinsulin antibodies

claim: Dimers and higher order complexes were detected by Western blotting with mAb anti-proinsulin, and all such higher bands collapsed to monomers upon reduction of disulfide bonds.
source: However, dimers and higher order complexes were detected by Western blotting of the identical samples with mAb anti-proinsulin (Figure 1D right), and all such higher bands, comprising the majority of intracellular proinsulin molecules, collapsed to monomers upon reduction of disulfide bonds (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by comparing nonreducing and reducing SDS-PAGE with anti-proinsulin immunoblotting

claim: Nearly all bands in the nonreduced ladder contained proinsulin, with molecular masses expected of disulfide-linked complexes as simple as homodimers, homotrimers, homotetramers, and homopentamers, as well as higher order complexes.
source: To confirm that the ladder of Western blotted bands detected by nonreducing SDS-PAGE specifically reflects disulfide-linked complexes of proinsulin, a similarly-generated sample was analyzed on a second-dimensional reducing SDS-PAGE, which demonstrated that nearly all bands in the nonreduced ladder contained proinsulin, with molecular masses expected of disulfide-linked complexes as simple as homodimers, homotrimers, homotetramers, and homopentamers, as well as higher order complexes (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis with first dimension nonreducing and second dimension reducing

claim: Disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes comprised 87% of all recovered proinsulin after PERK inhibition in INS1E cells.
source: Quantitatively these complexes comprised 87% of all recovered proinsulin.
evidence: Quantified from two-dimensional gel electrophoresis data

claim: In Akita mouse islets, the majority of proinsulin was recovered in aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes.
source: Indeed, Western blotting of nonreduced lysates of Akita mouse islets with anti-proinsulin demonstrated that the majority of proinsulin was recovered in aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes (Figure 1F), which were converted to monomeric proinsulin upon SDS-PAGE under reducing conditions.
evidence: Shown by nonreducing and reducing SDS-PAGE of Akita mouse islet lysates

claim: With increasing time of PERK inhibitor exposure, the majority of intracellular proinsulin accumulated in disulfide-linked complexes in β-cells.
source: With increasing time of exposure, the majority of intracellular proinsulin accumulated in disulfide-linked complexes in the ß-cells (Figure 2A second panel)
evidence: Shown by time-course experiment with PERK inhibitor treatment (0, 5, 10, 20 hr)

claim: Increased proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes were ultimately accompanied by decreased insulin content and decreased proinsulin secretion.
source: and this increase was ultimately accompanied by decreased insulin content (third panel) as well as decreased proinsulin secretion (final panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blotting of cell lysates and media after PERK inhibitor treatment

claim: Treatment of intracellular proinsulin dimers and larger complexes with AMS revealed that each of the oligomeric species in the ladder of bands shifted up after alkylation, indicating that each bears at least one unpaired cysteine thiol.
source: Significantly, treatment of intracellular proinsulin dimers and larger complexes with AMS, followed by nonreducing SDS-PAGE, revealed that each of the oligomeric species in the ladder of bands shifted up after alkylation, indicating that each of these forms still bears at least one unpaired cysteine thiol (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown by AMS alkylation of mouse islet lysates followed by nonreducing SDS-PAGE

claim: The presence of unpaired cysteine thiols in proinsulin oligomers provides a rationale for the propagation of disulfide-linked dimers into trimers, trimers into tetramers, etc.
source: These data provide a rationale for the propagation of disulfide-linked dimers into trimers, trimers into tetramers, etc.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all oligomeric species contain free thiols

claim: Pretreatment of cells with NEM before and during cell lysis results in the detection of dramatically less of the ladder of disulfide-linked proinsulin oligomers.
source: We found that pretreatment of cells with NEM before (and during) cell lysis results in the detection of dramatically less of the ladder of disulfide-linked proinsulin oligomers (Figure 2C)
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing lysates prepared with or without NEM pretreatment

claim: The relative abundance of the distinct disulfide-linked oligomeric species of proinsulin was essentially unchanged in cells that were either alkylated in situ with 20 mM N-ethyl maleimide prior to cell lysis, or not.
source: Nevertheless, the relative abundance of the distinct disulfide-linked oligomeric species of proinsulin was essentially unchanged in cells that were either alkylated in situ with 20 mM N-ethyl maleimide prior to cell lysis, or not (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown by comparing the ratio of oligomeric species with and without NEM pretreatment

claim: It is unlikely that the detection of aberrant disulfide-linked complexes of nonmutant proinsulin is an artifact of cell lysis conditions.
source: These data render it unlikely that the detection of aberrant disulfide-linked complexes of nonmutant proinsulin is an artifact of cell lysis conditions.
evidence: Inferred from NEM pretreatment experiments showing similar oligomer ratios

claim: Recombinant human proinsulin expressed in heterologous cells forms disulfide-linked dimers and higher-order complexes that accumulate to a dramatically higher level in cells treated overnight with PERK inhibitor.
source: Disulfide-linked proinsulin dimers along with a ladder of higher-order complexes already represented the majority of recombinant proinsulin species, and these forms accumulated to a dramatically higher level in cells treated overnight with PERK inhibitor (Figure 2D).
evidence: Shown by expressing human proinsulin in 293T cells and analyzing by nonreducing SDS-PAGE

claim: In several preparations of human islets from unrelated donors without a history of T2D, disulfide-linked dimers were prominent, along with a lesser abundance of higher-order complexes.
source: In several preparations, disulfide-linked dimers were prominent, along with a lesser abundance of higher-order complexes (Figure 3A right panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing SDS-PAGE of human islet lysates from multiple donors

claim: Overnight treatment of human islets with PERK inhibitor resulted in a further increase in higher order disulfide-linked complexes and an increase in total islet proinsulin.
source: Overnight treatment of human islets with PERK inhibitor resulted in a further increase in higher order disulfide-linked complexes (Figure 3A right panel, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and an increase in total islet proinsulin as revealed by reducing SDS-PAGE (Figure 3A left panel).
evidence: Shown by comparing vehicle-treated and PERK inhibitor-treated human islets

claim: Aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin dimers and higher complexes exist in human islets and their abundance responds to changes in environmental conditions within the ER.
source: These data indicate that aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin dimers and higher complexes exist in human islets and their abundance responds to changes in environmental conditions within the ER.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing changes in complex abundance with PERK inhibitor and SubAB treatment

claim: The immunodetection of both disulfide-linked dimers and higher-order complexes was blocked when pure human C-peptide competitor was included in the immunoblotting protocol.
source: The immunodetection of both disulfide-linked dimers and higher-order complexes was blocked when pure human C-peptide competitor was included in the immunoblotting protocol (Figure 3B), demonstrating specificity.
evidence: Demonstrated by peptide competition experiment

claim: In mouse islets, BiP was ≥90% destroyed within 2 hr after SubAB addition.
source: In mouse islets, BiP was ≥90% destroyed within 2 hr after SubAB addition (Figure 3C upper left)
evidence: Shown by immunoblotting for BiP after SubAB treatment

claim: BiP destruction by SubAB shifted the majority of proinsulin into larger disulfide-linked complexes in mouse islets.
source: and immunoblotting revealed that this treatment shifted the majority of proinsulin into larger disulfide-linked complexes (Figure 3C lower right).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing SDS-PAGE after SubAB treatment of mouse islets

claim: In a rodent β-cell line, improperly folded proinsulin began to migrate increasingly in disulfide-linked complexes 80 min after SubAB addition when only a portion of intracellular BiP had been destroyed.
source: Similarly, in a rodent ß-cell line, improperly folded proinsulin began to migrate increasingly in disulfide-linked complexes 80 min after SubAB addition when only a portion of intracellular BiP had been destroyed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown by time-course experiment with SubAB treatment in INS1E cells

claim: In the islets of humans not known to have T2D, improperly folded disulfide-linked proinsulin dimers were already apparent prior to SubAB addition, and an increase in larger-sized covalent proinsulin complexes was apparent at 4 hr of SubAB treatment.
source: In the islets of humans not known to have T2D, improperly folded disulfide-linked proinsulin dimers were already apparent prior to SubAB addition, and an increase in larger-sized covalent proinsulin complexes was apparent at 4 hr of SubAB treatment (Figure 3D lower panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-course SubAB treatment of human islets with nonreducing SDS-PAGE

claim: An acute increase in improper folding of human proinsulin occurs under conditions of BiP deficiency within the β-cell ER luminal environment, without any INS gene mutation.
source: These data demonstrate an acute increase in improper folding of human proinsulin, without any INS gene mutation, under conditions of BiP deficiency within the ß-cell ER luminal environment.
evidence: Inferred from SubAB experiments showing increased proinsulin complexes after BiP depletion

claim: Treatment of β-cells with GRP94 inhibitor (PU-WS13, 20 µM) even for 24 hr did not promote proinsulin disulfide-linked complex formation.
source: however, treatment of ß-cells with GRP94 inhibitor (PU-WS13, 20 µM) even for 24 hr did not promote proinsulin disulfide-linked complex formation, and did not exacerbate the proinsulin disulfide-linked complex formation that was triggered by an acute (3 hr) loss of BiP (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown by comparing GRP94 inhibitor treatment alone or in combination with SubAB

claim: After SubAB treatment of β-cells, the intracellular distribution of proinsulin shifted from its usual predominant juxtanuclear localization to a co-localization with the ER marker, calnexin.
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrated that after SubAB treatment of ß-cells, the intracellular distribution of proinsulin shifted from its usual predominant juxtanuclear localization [in the Golgi region from which newly-made insulin granules emerge (Haataja et al., 2013) to a co-localization with the ER marker, calnexin (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy with anti-proinsulin and anti-calnexin antibodies

claim: Proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes are misfolded and are retained within the ER compartment.
source: Altogether, these data strongly indicate that proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes are misfolded and are retained within the ER compartment.
evidence: Inferred from ER localization and lack of secretion of disulfide-linked complexes

claim: The predominant juxtanuclear Golgi-regional distribution of proinsulin is a feature of normal rodent islets.
source: The predominant juxtanuclear Golgi-regional distribution of proinsulin is a feature of normal rodent islets (Orci et al., 1985) (Figure 4C first set of panels).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence microscopy and supported by citation

claim: Within the first 4-5 months of life, leptin receptor mutant LepRdb/db mice in a C57BL/6 background become severely diabetic and develop a paucity of islet β-cells immunostainable for mature insulin.
source: Within the first 4–5 months of life, leptin receptor mutant LepRdb/db mice in a C57BL/6 background become severely diabetic and develop a paucity of islet ß-cells immunostainable for mature insulin — indeed, the fraction of islet ß-cells that exhibit little or no insulin immunostaining is known to increase by more than 5-fold compared to the islets of age-matched control mice (Ishida et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Proinsulin-positive immunostaining amongst the cells in diabetic LepRdb/db islets was more widespread and the intracellular distribution of proinsulin within these islet β-cells was no longer as concentrated in the Golgi region.
source: However, we observed that proinsulin-positive immunostaining amongst the cells in these diabetic islets was more widespread and the intracellular distribution of proinsulin within these islet ß-cells was no longer as concentrated in the Golgi region (Figure 4C second and third set of panels) with increased localization in the ER (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy of LepRdb/db mouse pancreas sections

claim: Limiting food intake of LepRdb/db animals can substantially increase the percentage of strongly insulin-immunopositive β-cells per islet.
source: It has been established that limiting food intake of these animals can substantially increase the percentage of strongly insulin-immunopositive ß-cells per islet (Ishida et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Upon fasting overnight, the islets of diabetic LepRdb/db mice exhibited a more robust immunostaining of mature insulin and a shift in intracellular proinsulin back towards a juxtanuclear distribution.
source: Indeed, upon fasting overnight, the islets of diabetic LepRdb/db mice exhibited a more robust immunostaining of mature insulin (Figure 4C fourth and fifth set of panels). Additionally, after fasting, there was a shift in intracellular proinsulin back towards a juxtanuclear distribution (Figure 4C fourth and fifth set of panels), consistent with previous reports (Alarcon et al., 2016).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy of fasted LepRdb/db mice and supported by citation

claim: In ad lib fed LepRdb/db diabetic mice, initial insulin depletion does not preclude ongoing proinsulin expression.
source: The data of Figure 4 strongly suggest that in ad lib fed LepRdb/db diabetic mice, initial insulin depletion does not preclude ongoing proinsulin expression
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence data showing proinsulin staining in insulin-depleted islets

claim: A shift of proinsulin distribution towards an ER-like pattern in LepRdb/db mice may suggest a stressed state that may be preventable and to some extent reversible by limiting β-cell secretory stimulation.
source: moreover, a shift of proinsulin distribution towards an ER-like pattern (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) may suggest a stressed state that may be preventable and to some extent reversible by limiting ß-cell secretory stimulation (i.e., 'ß-cell rest') (Ishida et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence data and supported by citation

claim: In prediabetic LepRdb/db mice (4 and 6 weeks of age with random blood glucose levels of 101 and 118 mg/dL), >90% of proinsulin molecules were entangled in disulfide-linked dimers and higher-order complexes.
source: We examined proinsulin in the islet lysates of 5 additional prediabetic LepRdb/db mice — all were similar to the islets of two animals shown in Figures 4D (4 and 6 weeks of age with random blood glucose levels of 101 and 118 mg/dL, respectively) containing a large steady state level of proinsulin (seen upon Western blotting of reducing SDS-PAGE) with >90% of molecules entangled in disulfide-linked dimers and higher-order complexes (seen by Western blotting upon nonreducing SDS-PAGE, Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing SDS-PAGE of islet lysates from young LepRdb/db mice

claim: Accumulation of misfolded proinsulin in the ER of LepRdb/db β-cells was always present before the onset of diabetes.
source: Accumulation of misfolded proinsulin in the ER of LepRdb/db ß-cells was always present before the onset of diabetes.
evidence: Demonstrated across multiple prediabetic LepRdb/db mice with normal or mildly elevated blood glucose

claim: Improperly folded proinsulin was detectable in WT mouse islets, albeit at a much lower abundance than in LepRdb/db islets.
source: Importantly, improperly folded proinsulin was also detectable in WT mouse islets, albeit at a much lower abundance (Figure 4D lane 4).
evidence: Shown by nonreducing SDS-PAGE of wild-type mouse islet lysates

claim: Pancreatic islets from LepR-Nkx2.1 KO mice (deficient for leptin receptor in the hypothalamus but not in the islets) demonstrated markedly increased abundance of disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes with >90% of proinsulin entangled in such complexes.
source: Here too, pancreatic islets from these hyperphagic, obese, glucose intolerant animals demonstrated markedly increased abundance of disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes with >90% of proinsulin entangled in such complexes (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing SDS-PAGE of islet lysates from LepR-Nkx2.1 KO mice

claim: An increase in improper proinsulin folding in leptin receptor-deficient animals is secondary to a prediabetic state and unrelated to leptin receptor function in β-cells.
source: These data indicate that an increase in improper proinsulin folding in leptin receptor-deficient animals is secondary to a prediabetic state and unrelated to leptin receptor function in ß-cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of LepRdb/db and LepR-Nkx2.1 KO mice showing similar proinsulin misfolding

claim: Improper proinsulin folding is already detectable at a time associated with ER stress response but before onset of chronic hyperglycemia associated with pancreatic insulin deficiency.
source: Crucially, these data also demonstrate that improper proinsulin folding is already detectable at a time that has been associated with ER stress response (Herbert and Laybutt, 2016) but before onset of chronic hyperglycemia associated with pancreatic insulin deficiency that has been attributed to a loss of functional ß-cell mass [regardless of whether this is due to de-differentiation (Bensellam et al., 2018) or ß-cell death (Eizirik and Millard, 2014; Kanekura et al., 2015; Marchetti et al., 2012; Papa, 2012) or both].
evidence: Inferred from data showing proinsulin misfolding in prediabetic mice and supported by multiple citations

claim: The levels of p58ipk began to increase in ad lib fed LepRdb/db mice even before the animals have reached a random blood glucose of 160 mg/dL.
source: Based on the work of Laybutt et al. (2007), we examined islet protein content of p58ipk (encoded by DNAJC3) as a reliable marker of islet ER stress response, and found that the levels of this ER co-chaperone of BiP began to increase in ad lib fed LepRdb/db mice even before the animals have reached a random blood glucose of 160 mg/dL (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting for p58ipk in islet lysates from LepRdb/db mice at different stages and supported by citation

claim: Islet p58ipk protein levels tended to be elevated in LepR-Nkx2.1 KO mice.
source: Islet p58ipk protein levels also tended to be elevated in LepR-Nkx2.1 KO mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shown by immunoblotting for p58ipk in islet lysates from LepR-Nkx2.1 KO mice

claim: In young, normoglycemic homozygous LepRdb/db male mice destined for diabetes, proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes were increased slightly above the level observed in heterozygous LepRdb/+ males, and islet insulin levels were similarly increased.
source: In the islets of young, normoglycemic homozygous LepRdb/db male mice that are destined for diabetes, proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes (Figure 5C upper left panel) were increased slightly above the level observed in heterozygous LepRdb/+ males (that do not progress to diabetes), and islet insulin levels were similarly increased (lower left panels).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing and reducing SDS-PAGE of islet lysates from young LepRdb/db mice

claim: With a random blood glucose level in the mid 200's (mg/dL) in LepRdb/db mice, islet proinsulin was notably increased and comprised >90% of disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes whereas simultaneously, islet insulin levels were dramatically decreased.
source: With a random blood glucose level in the mid 200's (mg/dL), islet proinsulin was notably increased (Figure 5C upper second panel) and comprised >90% of disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes (upper first panel) whereas simultaneously, islet insulin levels were dramatically decreased (lower left panels).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing and reducing SDS-PAGE of islet lysates from LepRdb/db mice with mid-range hyperglycemia

claim: With a random blood glucose level >500 mg/dL in LepRdb/db mice, islet proinsulin and insulin levels were both severely diminished.
source: With a random blood glucose level >500 mg/dL, islet proinsulin and insulin levels were both severely diminished (Figure 5C left panels).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting of islet lysates from severely diabetic LepRdb/db mice

claim: In female LepRdb/db mice with a random blood glucose ranging from 156 to 294 mg/dL, insulin levels declined compared to the LepRdb/+ control, but islet proinsulin was increased and >90% was entangled in disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes.
source: In female LepRdb/db mice with a random blood glucose ranging from 156 to 294 mg/dL, insulin levels declined compared to the LepRdb/+ control (Figure 5C lower right panels). However, for females in this glycemic range, as in males, islet proinsulin was increased (Figure 5 upper right panel) and once again, >90% was entangled in disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes (Figure 5 upper third panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing and reducing SDS-PAGE of islet lysates from female LepRdb/db mice

claim: In female LepRdb/db mice with a random blood glucose of 455 mg/dL, both proinsulin and insulin were severely diminished indicating islet decompensation.
source: Additionally, with a random blood glucose of 455 mg/dL, both proinsulin and insulin were severely diminished (Figure 5C last two sets of panels) indicating islet decompensation.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting of islet lysates from severely diabetic female LepRdb/db mice

claim: During progression to diabetes in LepRdb/db mice, intracellular proinsulin distribution that initially displayed a prominent juxtanuclear pattern with good co-localization to the Golgi region tended to shift towards a staining pattern that was more spread in the cytoplasm, with increased co-localization with the ER marker, calnexin.
source: During this progression to diabetes, intracellular proinsulin distribution that initially displayed a prominent juxtanuclear pattern with good co-localization to the Golgi region (GM130 Golgi marker) tended to shift towards a staining pattern that was more spread in the cytoplasm, with increased co-localization with the ER marker, calnexin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy with proinsulin, GM130, and calnexin markers

claim: Even in the fully diabetic state, there appeared to be increased juxtanuclear (Golgi-like) proinsulin distribution after overnight fasting in LepRdb/db mice.
source: although even in the fully diabetic state there appeared to be increased juxtanuclear (Golgi-like) proinsulin distribution after overnight fasting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy of fasted diabetic LepRdb/db mice

claim: Cys(A20) and Cys(B19) are two of the three most reactive thiols of proinsulin, and they initiate covalent association of B- and A-domains that are required for proinsulin export from the ER.
source: Cys(A20) and Cys(B19) are two of the three most reactive thiols of proinsulin, and they initiate covalent association of B- and A-domains that are required for proinsulin export from the ER (Haataja et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: A human mutant proinsulin that retains only two cysteines, named 'keep-B19/A20' cannot undergo efficient intramolecular oxidation in the redox environment of the pancreatic β-cell ER.
source: Nevertheless, in the redox environment of the pancreatic ß-cell ER, a human mutant proinsulin that retains only two cysteines, named 'keep-B19/A20' cannot undergo efficient intramolecular oxidation (Haataja et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Each of the myc-tagged human proinsulins keep-B7/A7, keep-A6/A11, and keep-B19/A20 exhibited free thiol availability as determined by alkylation with AMS.
source: Indeed, each of the myc-tagged human proinsulins keep-B7/A7 and keep-A6/A11, in addition to keep-B19/A20, exhibited free thiol availability as determined by alkylation with AMS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by AMS alkylation experiments showing band shifts

claim: Two-cysteine mutant human proinsulins cannot be exported from the ER and are excellent ERAD substrates in pancreatic β-cells.
source: Because these two-cysteine mutant human proinsulins cannot be exported from the ER and are excellent ERAD substrates in pancreatic ß-cells (Haataja et al., 2016), these molecules were largely undetected by immunoblotting.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: In β-cells treated with proteasome inhibitor (MG132 for 7 hr), myc-tagged proinsulin monomers were detected in all cases of two-cysteine mutants.
source: However, in ß-cells treated with proteasome inhibitor (MG132 for 7 hr), myc-tagged proinsulin monomers were detected in all cases (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting after MG132 treatment

claim: The keep-B19/A20 construct recapitulated the situation in which the majority of molecules migrated as disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes.
source: Remarkably, not only were these constructs capable of forming disulfide-linked proinsulin homodimers, but the keep-B19/A20 construct in particular recapitulated the situation in which the majority of molecules migrated as disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing SDS-PAGE of cells expressing keep-B19/A20

claim: The behavior of keep-B19/A20 forming disulfide-linked complexes was also observed upon expression in 293 T cells that lack endogenous proinsulin, and these complexes appeared quite similar to those observed in human islets.
source: With or without MG132, this behavior was also observed upon expression in 293 T cells that lack endogenous proinsulin (Figure 6B), and these complexes appeared quite similar to those observed in human islets (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by expressing keep-B19/A20 in 293T cells and comparing to human islet data

claim: Of the mutant human proinsulins that retain only one set of potential disulfide partners, only keep-B19/A20 could efficiently recreate the entire ladder of disulfide-linked complexes similar to that seen for wildtype proinsulin.
source: Once again, of the mutant human proinsulins that retain only one set of potential disulfide partners, only keep-B19/A20 could efficiently recreate the entire ladder of disulfide-linked complexes similar to that seen for wildtype proinsulin, irrespective of the presence or absence of an engineered myc epitope tag in the C-peptide (Figure 6C left panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing different two-cysteine mutants by nonreducing SDS-PAGE

claim: Lose-B19/A20 did not efficiently recreate the ladder of disulfide-linked complexes despite entrapment in the ER in a proinsulin construct bearing four Cys residues.
source: However, lose-B19/A20 did not efficiently recreate the ladder of disulfide-linked complexes despite entrapment in the ER in a proinsulin construct bearing four Cys residues.
evidence: Demonstrated by nonreducing SDS-PAGE of cells expressing lose-B19/A20

claim: The Cys(B19)/Cys(A20) pair is both necessary and sufficient for efficient propagation of disulfide-linked complexes of improperly-folded proinsulin.
source: These data indicate that the Cys(B19)/Cys(A20) pair is both necessary and sufficient for efficient propagation of disulfide-linked complexes of improperly-folded proinsulin.
evidence: Inferred from experiments comparing different cysteine mutants

claim: All 2-Cys proinsulin mutants have the capability to at least weakly form a covalent dimer.
source: In these experiments, we were struck by the observations 1) that all 2-Cys proinsulin mutants have the capability to at least weakly form a covalent dimer, which is essential to the further propagation of these improperly folded complexes into trimers, tetramers, and higher order complexes (Figure 2B)
evidence: Observed from experiments with two-cysteine mutants

claim: A small fraction of proinsulin dimers appeared to remain even after reducing SDS-PAGE.
source: and 2) a small fraction of proinsulin dimers appeared to remain even after reducing SDS-PAGE (Figure 4D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Observed in multiple experiments with reducing SDS-PAGE

claim: Five of the six Cys residues could make a homotypic covalent association, but Cys(A7) preferred not to make the disulfide bond.
source: Although five of the six Cys residues could make a homotypic covalent association, Cys(A7) preferred not to make the disulfide bond (Figure 7A left panel; quantified in Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by expressing single-cysteine proinsulin mutants and analyzing by nonreducing SDS-PAGE

claim: Cys(B19) not only covalently homodimerized with exuberance but this Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) bond could not be broken at room temperature in SDS-gel sample buffer even in the presence of 200 mM dithiothreitol.
source: More significantly, Cys(B19) not only covalently homodimerized with exuberance (Figure 7A left panel) but this Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) bond could not be broken at room temperature in SDS-gel sample buffer even in the presence of 200 mM dithiothreitol (Figure 7A right panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by expressing keep-B19 mutant and attempting reduction with DTT

claim: A Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) disulfide bond between proinsulin monomers predisposes to strongly-associated covalent complexes that are automatically misfolded by omitting the crucial intramolecular Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) disulfide bond.
source: These data indicate that a Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) disulfide bond between proinsulin monomers predisposes to strongly-associated covalent complexes that are automatically misfolded by omitting the crucial intramolecular Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) disulfide bond, which leaves the critical reactive Cys(A20) residue unpaired and available for further disulfide infidelity.
evidence: Inferred from the resistance of Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) bonds to reduction and the presence of free Cys(A20)

claim: A Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) initiating event can form a nidus for assembly of larger misfolded disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes.
source: Such an initiating event can thus form a nidus for assembly of larger misfolded disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the properties of Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) bonds and the presence of free thiols in oligomers

claim: Pancreatic β-cell ER stress is a recognized part of type 2 diabetes.
source: yet MIDY is a rare disease. Of far broader significance is the β-cell failure that accompanies 'garden variety' T2D without INS mutations, and though the molecular pathogenesis of insulin deficiency in this condition remains murky (Halban et al., 2014), β-cell ER stress is a recognized part of the disease.
evidence: Supported by citation and established scientific knowledge

claim: β-cells compensate for insulin resistance by increasing insulin production that may eventually overwhelm the ER capacity for efficient protein folding, thereby provoking β-cell ER stress.
source: It has been suggested that β-cells compensate for insulin resistance by increasing insulin production that may eventually overwhelm the ER capacity for efficient protein folding, thereby provoking β-cell ER stress (Back and Kaufman, 2012; Eizirik et al., 2008; Herbert and Laybutt, 2016; Papa, 2012; Rabhi et al., 2014; Volchuk and Ron, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: In the absence of INS gene mutations, it has not been established the extent to which proinsulin misfolding is present in the early triggering stages of T2D, including prediabetes and mild dysglycemia.
source: However, in the absence of INS gene mutations, it has not been established the extent to which proinsulin misfolding is present in the early triggering stages of T2D, including prediabetes and mild dysglycemia — prior to more obvious islet failure including β-cell degranulation and dedifferentiation (Accili et al., 2016; Kahn, 1998; Kahn et al., 2009) that occurs in both human islets (Cinti et al., 2016) and rodent islets (Ishida et al., 2017).
evidence: Identifies a gap in knowledge supported by multiple citations

claim: Proinsulin misfolding provides a status report on the health of the β-cell ER folding environment.
source: There is strong reason to believe that proinsulin disulfide-linked complex formation provides a status report on the health of the ß-cell ER folding environment.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing changes in proinsulin complexes with ER perturbations

claim: The activity of ER stress (UPR) sensor proteins are required to actively maintain a proper ER chaperone and oxidoreductase environment for optimal proinsulin folding.
source: Many studies point to the idea that the activity of ER stress (UPR) sensor proteins are required to actively maintain a proper ER chaperone and oxidoreductase environment for optimal proinsulin folding (Harding et al., 2012; Hassler et al., 2015; Sowers et al., 2018; Tsuchiya et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: Protein disulfide isomerase is one of the ER luminal factors that regulates the balance of proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes and monomers.
source: Recent work indicates that protein disulfide isomerase is one of the ER luminal factors that regulates the balance of proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes and monomers (Jang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work

claim: BiP plays a central role in ER stress sensing.
source: Additionally, BiP plays a central role in ER stress sensing (Amin-Wetzel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Even a modest decrease of BiP levels results in improperly folded proinsulin rapidly accumulating in disulfide-linked complexes.
source: We show here that even a modest decrease of BiP levels results in improperly folded proinsulin rapidly accumulating in disulfide-linked complexes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), supporting that proinsulin folding is highly sensitive to changes in the ER folding environment
evidence: Demonstrated by SubAB experiments showing rapid increase in proinsulin complexes

claim: Proinsulin folding is highly sensitive to changes in the ER folding environment, which can include excessive proinsulin biosynthesis, altered chaperone and/or oxidoreductase expression, and changes in the rate of clearance of misfolded proinsulin molecules.
source: supporting that proinsulin folding is highly sensitive to changes in the ER folding environment, which can include excessive proinsulin biosynthesis, altered chaperone and/or oxidoreductase expression, and changes in the rate of clearance of misfolded proinsulin molecules (Arunagiri et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citations

claim: ER luminal factors are needed to enhance the efficiency of formation of the proinsulin intramolecular Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) disulfide bond.
source: We believe that these and other ER luminal factors are needed to enhance the efficiency of formation of the proinsulin intramolecular Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) disulfide bond.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing importance of Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) and effects of ER perturbations

claim: The intramolecular Cys(B19)-Cys(A20) disulfide bond is critical to additional native proinsulin disulfide pairing.
source: Not only is this internal disulfide critical to additional native proinsulin disulfide pairing (Haataja et al., 2016) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Complexes bearing a homotypic Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) covalent bond are likely to be the most difficult to successfully isomerize.
source: However, those complexes bearing a homotypic Cys(B19)-Cys(B19) covalent bond are likely to be the most difficult to successfully isomerize, as this bond cannot be broken in vitro even in the presence of SDS plus 200 mM DTT (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing resistance to reduction

claim: Beginning around 4-5 months of life in LepRdb/db mice, after hyperglycemia has appeared, β-cells appear to be in the early stages of dedifferentiation.
source: What has recently emerged using the LepRdb/db mouse model, is that beginning around 4–5 months of life, after hyperglycemia has appeared, ß-cells appear to be in the early stages of dedifferentiation (Ishida et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: With a similar time course to β-cell dedifferentiation, β-cell apoptosis may occur in parallel in LepRdb/db mice.
source: and with a similar time course, ß-cell apoptosis may occur in parallel (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Important islet changes occur considerably before β-cell dedifferentiation and apoptosis in LepRdb/db mice, including β-cell ER stress response activation.
source: However, clearly there are important islet changes that occur considerably before these events (Do et al., 2016) including ß-cell ER stress response activation (Figure 5A,B) (Herbert and Laybutt, 2016).
evidence: Demonstrated by p58ipk data and supported by citations

claim: Throughout the first, compensated stage of diabetes progression in LepRdb/db mice, improperly folded proinsulin is increased but islet insulin content is still robust.
source: Our work highlights that throughout the first, compensated stage, improperly folded proinsulin is increased but islet insulin content is still robust (Figures 4D and 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blotting data from young LepRdb/db mice

claim: In the second, decompensating stage of diabetes progression in LepRdb/db mice, islet proinsulin levels are further increased, but much of this is improperly folded proinsulin in the ER, and islet insulin levels begin to drop.
source: In the second, decompensating stage, islet proinsulin levels are actually further increased, but much of this is improperly folded proinsulin in the ER, and at this stage, islet insulin levels begin to drop (Figure 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blotting data from LepRdb/db mice with mid-range hyperglycemia

claim: At a high level of hyperglycemia in LepRdb/db mice, both proinsulin and insulin steady state levels are low, which correlates with the time when β-cell dedifferentiation and β-cell death have been reported.
source: It is at a still higher level of hyperglycemia that both proinsulin and insulin steady state levels are low (Figure 8), which correlates with the time when ß-cell dedifferentiation and ß-cell death have been reported.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blotting data from severely diabetic LepRdb/db mice and correlated with literature

claim: Even when proinsulin and insulin levels are low in severely diabetic LepRdb/db mice, the low-level proinsulin protein that is still expressed is recovered >90% in aberrant disulfide linked complexes.
source: It should be noted that even at this time, the low-level proinsulin protein that is still expressed is recovered >90% in aberrant disulfide linked complexes
evidence: Observed from Western blotting data of severely diabetic mice

claim: Partial restoration of secretory pathway function in severely diabetic LepRdb/db mice requires β-cell rest.
source: and even partial restoration of secretory pathway function requires ß-cell rest (Alarcon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Throughout the progression of β-cell stress in T2D, quality control of proinsulin anterograde export from the ER is maintained.
source: We suspect that throughout the progression of ß-cell stress in T2D, quality control of proinsulin anterograde export from the ER is nevertheless maintained.
evidence: Inferred from observations that secreted proinsulin lacks disulfide-linked complexes

claim: Secreted proinsulin cannot be alkylated with AMS and is not recovered in disulfide-linked complexes, even from islets or cells in which proinsulin has accumulated intracellularly in disulfide-linked complexes at massive levels.
source: We note that we have been unable to detect secreted proinsulin that can be alkylated with AMS, or that is recovered in disulfide-linked complexes, even from islets or cells in which proinsulin has accumulated intracellularly in disulfide-linked complexes at massive levels.
evidence: Demonstrated across multiple experiments examining secreted proinsulin

claim: Patients with T2D are known to have abnormally high levels of immunoreactive proinsulin in the circulation.
source: However, experiments such as these will need to be rigorously tested with islets from human T2D subjects, as these patients are known to have abnormally high levels of immunoreactive proinsulin in the circulation (Porte and Kahn, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Disulfide-linked complexes of proinsulin are one of the earliest tissue biomarkers indicating β-cell secretory pathway dysfunction, which is associated with ER stress and ultimate insulin deficiency that occurs in the natural progression of T2D.
source: Nevertheless, the data presented herein establish disulfide-linked complexes of proinsulin as one of the earliest tissue biomarkers indicating ß-cell secretory pathway dysfunction, which is associated with ER stress and ultimate insulin deficiency that occurs in the natural progression of T2D.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive data showing proinsulin complexes appear early in disease progression

claim: A chronic increase in insulin secretory demand over time leads to depletion of β-cell secretory granule reserves despite a dramatic compensatory increase in secretory pathway activity.
source: What is observed is that a chronic increase in insulin secretory demand over time leads to depletion of ß-cell secretory granule reserves despite a dramatic compensatory increase in secretory pathway activity (Alarcon et al., 2016; Rustenbeck, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Pancreatic sections of human subjects with T2D show a marked increase of ER volume density in β-cells with an induction of ER stress markers triggered by high glucose exposure.
source: By electron microscopy, pancreatic sections of human subjects with T2D show a marked increase of ER volume density in β-cells with an induction of ER stress markers triggered by high glucose exposure (Marchetti et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Similar indicators of ER stress have been established in the β-cells of animal models such as leptin receptor-deficient diabetic mice.
source: Similar indicators of ER stress have been established in the β-cells of animal models (Yang et al., 2016), such as leptin receptor-deficient diabetic mice [known as LepRdb/db (Diani et al., 1984; Laybutt et al., 2007; Like and Chick, 1970) that develop insulin resistance progressing to T2D, which is linked to overeating.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: Hypersynthesis of proinsulin is a condition proposed to increase proinsulin misfolding.
source: Hypersynthesis of proinsulin (Arunagiri et al., 2018; Back et al., 2009) is a condition proposed to increase proinsulin misfolding (Liu et al., 2005; Scheuner et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: Proinsulin misfolding can promote ER stress with abnormal β-cell ER expansion.
source: — which can promote ER stress with abnormal ß-cell ER expansion —
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between proinsulin misfolding and ER stress

claim: Suppression of proinsulin protein synthesis alleviates β-cell ER stress.
source: whereas suppression of proinsulin protein synthesis actually alleviates ß-cell ER stress (Szabat et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: Insulin-deficiency caused directly by proinsulin misfolding has been proved unequivocally in an autosomal-dominant form of diabetes known as Mutant INS-gene-induced Diabetes of Youth (MIDY).
source: Insulin-deficiency caused directly by proinsulin misfolding has been proved unequivocally in an autosomal-dominant form of diabetes known as Mutant INS-gene-induced Diabetes of Youth (MIDY) (Liu et al., 2010b), which occurs in patients bearing one mutant and one wild-type INS allele (Liu et al., 2015; Støy et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work

claim: The disease in humans with MIDY is pathogenetically identical to that seen in the mutant Akita diabetic mouse or Munich MIDY Pig.
source: The disease in humans is pathogenetically identical to that seen in the mutant Akita diabetic mouse (Izumi et al., 2003) or Munich MIDY Pig (Blutke et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: Akita mice develop diabetes despite expressing three alleles encoding WT proinsulin in addition to the one encoding mutant proinsulin.
source: Ordinarily the expression of only one WT INS allele would be sufficient to avoid diabetes, but Akita mice develop diabetes despite expressing three alleles encoding WT proinsulin in addition to the one encoding mutant proinsulin (Liu et al., 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work

claim: In MIDY, it is the expression of misfolded proinsulin that triggers diabetes.
source: Both preclinical and clinical data prove that in MIDY, it is the expression of misfolded proinsulin that triggers diabetes; yet MIDY is a rare disease.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge from preclinical and clinical data
